title: Animal Control

jokes.text: Oh, this is a napkin where I wrote down a cool name for a dog. 'Bark Obama.' Right?
jokes.setup: Tour of Animal Control office highlights mundane features
jokes.punchline: 'Bark Obama' — a dog name pun on Barack Obama, presented as a point of pride
jokes.explanation: The pun itself is simple but the framing sells it — that this napkin is being presented as a meaningful artifact of the office tour, and Harris says 'Right?' fishing for validation, is what makes it land. The pride is the joke as much as the wordplay. Solidly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: And here we have our holding area for various animals we've brought in.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: This is a raccoon, this is a possum, and this is a... well, we're not entirely sure what this one is.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: Been here for three weeks and nobody's been able to identify it.

jokes.text: Oh. Yo. Yeah. We found this bird outside. We tried to turn it into a work whistle, like in the beginning of The Flintstones. Tougher than it looked, though.
jokes.setup: Tour of Animal Control department introduces us to the two employees
jokes.punchline: Their grand ambition was to turn a live bird into a Flintstones-style work whistle, and it didn't work out
jokes.explanation: Perfectly absurdist character establishment. The Flintstones reference is unexpected, specific, and reveals everything about these characters' stoned logic. 'Tougher than it looked, though' is a masterful deadpan understatement — the entire premise is insane but delivered matter-of-factly. Strong character integration: only these two would think this was a reasonable endeavor.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: It's just a terrible dog pun on a napkin

jokes.text: There's more than one way to skin a cat. / Four. There's four ways to skin a cat. Regular blade--
jokes.setup: Leslie uses the idiom 'there's more than one way to skin a cat' charitably about the department
jokes.punchline: One of the Animal Control employees corrects her with specific expertise: 'Four. There's four ways to skin a cat. Regular blade--'
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect comedic subversion. Leslie's idiom is used to give these employees the benefit of the doubt; they respond by literalizing the idiom and demonstrating specific, disturbing knowledge about it. The trailing 'Regular blade--' mid-sentence before being interrupted is expert structure — it implies even more specificity was coming. The economy is outstanding: maximum comic payload with minimal words. Easily the strongest joke in the Animal Control cold open sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 2
dialogue.line: They tried to use a live bird as a cartoon whistle

jokes.text: Yeah, we got, like, a huge vermin problem. I mean, we've been meaning to call somebody about it, but you know, nobody get on the phone. / You're the people you would be calling. / That is so trippy.
jokes.setup: Harris explains there's a huge vermin problem and they've been meaning to call someone
jokes.punchline: Leslie points out they ARE animal control; the guy finds this revelation mind-blowing
jokes.explanation: 'That is so trippy' is a perfect comedic button. The joke works on multiple levels: their incompetence, their altered state, and the fact that this revelation genuinely seems to blow their minds. Strong character integration — this reaction is completely specific to stoned incompetents. Very quotable delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You're pot-head losers running a miserable suck hole.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks! We try our best.

jokes.text: Ow! You're fired! You're fired! The whole department is fired. Ow, this hurts! This was one of my running feet!
jokes.setup: Leslie is trapped in a coyote trap and in pain
jokes.punchline: She tries to assert authority while clearly incapacitated, and the detail 'This was one of my running feet!' adds absurd specificity
jokes.explanation: Leslie trying to maintain authority while in obvious pain is great character comedy. 'This was one of my running feet!' is a wonderfully specific absurd detail — implying she has a designated running foot is endearingly odd. Strong Leslie characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker
dialogue.line: Well, there's more than one way to skin a cat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Actually, there are several ways. You could use a knife, you could use a box cutter, you could use a—

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I get it.

jokes.text: - Yo, let's go to Jamaica. - No, we should go to Jamaica. / Oh, is that what you said? / Yeah, dog.
jokes.setup: Their boss has just been hurt by their trap and fired them
jokes.punchline: They immediately pivot to planning a Jamaica trip, then act like they each had the same idea independently
jokes.explanation: Good scene-closing beat that reinforces their complete obliviousness. The 'Oh is that what you said?' misunderstanding between two people who said the same thing simultaneously is a nice character touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ow! What the—

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker
dialogue.line: Ma'am, you need to stay still. The more you struggle, the worse it gets.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How is this here? Why do we have a coyote trap in the middle of the office?

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker
dialogue.line: We've had reports of coyotes in the area. We set these traps to keep the city safe.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, congratulations. You've trapped a Department of Parks and Recreation Deputy Director instead.

jokes.text: Last night, I watched a movie with Diane and the girls in which an orange fish is separated from his father. The children were sniffling, which I believed to be due to the sad nature of the film. I was wrong.
jokes.setup: Ron is clearly sick and sweating. He's asked about fluids.
jokes.punchline: Ron explains he got sick from Diane's kids watching Finding Nemo — delivered as a stoic military-style after-action report
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The structure is flawless: setup establishes a movie (never named but obviously Finding Nemo via 'orange fish separated from his father'), builds to what seems like an emotional observation about children crying, then the hard pivot to 'I was wrong' — delivered in Ron's characteristic flat affect — reframes the sniffling as illness. The joke works on three levels simultaneously: Ron's stoicism, his unfamiliarity with children's culture, and the comic misdirection. 'I was wrong' as the entire punchline is masterful economy. Extremely Ron-specific — this could only be this character.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: We should call animal control about this vermin problem.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 2
dialogue.line: We ARE animal control.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: Whoa...

jokes.text: Usually, I take it neat, but I will make an exception in the name of health.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Ron he needs to drink water
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he normally drinks water 'neat' (like whiskey), but will make an exception
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly economic Ron joke. Applying whiskey-drinking terminology to water is perfectly in character — Ron views all consumables through the lens of his whiskey preferences. Short, punchy, immediately tells you everything about the character. Very quotable. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: One of my running feet!

jokes.text: Please turn the thermostat up to 90 and leave me alone.
jokes.setup: Leslie is mothering Ron and telling him to remove layers and see a doctor
jokes.punchline: Ron's counter-demand is to crank the heat to 90 degrees and be left in peace
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron stubbornness played for laughs. The specific number (90 degrees) makes it funnier than a generic refusal. Good character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: Dude, you know what we should do? We should totally go to that new taco place on Fifth Street.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 2
dialogue.line: Whoa, man, that's exactly what I was just about to say. We should go to that new taco place on Fifth Street.

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 1
dialogue.line: No way, seriously?

dialogue.speaker: Animal Control Worker 2
dialogue.line: Yeah man, we're like totally on the same wavelength.

jokes.text: Uh, 'Spasm.' No, 'Butter Face'! / Very good!
jokes.setup: Ben and/or Andy are asked to identify a cologne scent by name
jokes.punchline: The cologne is called 'Butter Face' — an absurd/vulgar name for a luxury product
jokes.explanation: Both cologne names are funny — 'Spasm' as a guess and 'Butter Face' (a slang insult) as an actual product name. The juxtaposition of high-end perfume culture with vulgar naming convention is a good absurdist touch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Water. I drink it neat.

jokes.text: Dennis Feinstein belongs to a new generation of wealth-- rappers, tech geniuses, X games medallists, and of course, 'scent artists.' The man owns a Rolexus. It's a Lexus filled with Rolexes. What's the point of that? To have it, which he does.
jokes.setup: Tom introduces Dennis Feinstein as a potential donor
jokes.punchline: The 'Rolexus' — a Lexus filled with Rolexes — climaxes with 'To have it, which he does' as an explanation
jokes.explanation: The 'Rolexus' is a genuinely inventive absurdist creation. The exchange 'What's the point of that?' / 'To have it, which he does' is perfectly structured — the question seems reasonable, the answer is both circular and completely accurate, and the tacked-on 'which he does' adds an extra comedic beat. This reads as Tom-specific: only Tom would deliver this with admiration rather than mockery. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't get sick. But when I do, I don't waste time with your over-the-counter remedies and your health fads. I just power through it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Last week I had a fever of 103. I went to work, cut down a tree, and watched the film about the clownfish and his son without saying the title once. Referred to it only as 'that animated ocean journey.'

jokes.text: I already took what I call a 'dwyer shower.' I rubbed my armpits with air fresheners.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Andy to take a shower before the important meeting
jokes.punchline: Andy has invented an alternative to showering involving rubbing air fresheners on his armpits, and he's named it after himself
jokes.explanation: The 'Dwyer shower' is a fantastic piece of character comedy. Andy naming his own lazy hygiene shortcut after himself is perfectly on-brand. The specificity (air fresheners on armpits) is both disgusting and completely believable for the character. 'New car' as the implied scent result is a great visual/olfactory punchline. Very quotable and highly character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, this one is called 'Eau de Desperation.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, that's definitely me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, wait. This is 'Regret and Broken Dreams.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's also me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, last one: 'I Made a Huge Mistake.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Nailed it.

jokes.text: New car. [reaction beat — someone smells Andy after the 'Dwyer shower']
jokes.setup: Andy announces he rubbed his armpits with air fresheners
jokes.punchline: The immediate smell-test result: 'New car' — implying he smells exactly like a car air freshener
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Dwyer shower joke. The economy is extraordinary — two words deliver the punchline of the preceding joke. The callback structure (setup then immediate verification) is clean and efficient. Rewatch bonus because you'll look for who delivers the line.

jokes.text: Friend of mine, bit of an alcoholic, a little grabby, either a war hero or war criminal, depending on who you ask, but a good dude.
jokes.setup: Jamm claims he has the perfect candidate for Animal Control director
jokes.punchline: His glowing recommendation is a litany of red flags: alcoholic, grabby, war hero OR war criminal
jokes.explanation: Good escalating character comedy. The structure builds nicely: 'alcoholic' → 'grabby' → the brilliant 'war hero or war criminal, depending on who you ask' which is both funny and reveals Jamm's complete indifference to basic vetting. 'But a good dude' as the dismissive summary is perfect. The 'depending on who you ask' is the comedic peak.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, you really need to shower.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But Leslie, I already did a Sniff-wash this morning.

jokes.text: How do you know him? / I do his teeth. / A few coffee stains up front, but his canines are insane.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how Jamm knows this 'war hero or war criminal'
jokes.punchline: Jamm is his dentist and recommends him based on the quality of his canine teeth
jokes.explanation: Strong Jamm character joke. His dental credentials being the basis for professional networking is perfectly on-brand. 'His canines are insane' is a great specific detail — using dog-related dental terminology for a would-be Animal Control director is a nice accidental double meaning.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I have a candidate for you. He's extremely qualified.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: He's been fired from every job he's ever had.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: He's currently under investigation by the FBI.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: And he's only been to prison twice.

jokes.text: Gosh, Jeremy, he sounds perfect. Are his gums great too? / Oh, yeah. They are excellent, beet red. / I was being sarcastic.
jokes.setup: Leslie sarcastically asks if his gums are good too
jokes.punchline: Jamm enthusiastically confirms: 'Excellent, beet red' — not catching the sarcasm at all, and Leslie has to clarify
jokes.explanation: Nice comedic beat. Jamm's obliviousness to sarcasm when it touches his professional domain (dentistry) is perfectly in character. 'Beet red' as a positive dental assessment is a funny specific detail — beet red gums are actually not great. Leslie's flat 'I was being sarcastic' is a good straight-man button.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: He has no teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that's one less thing to floss.

jokes.text: This whole place runs on dibs.
jokes.setup: Leslie is outraged that city council appointments are made by taking turns rather than merit
jokes.punchline: A councilman matter-of-factly explains the entire system: 'dibs'
jokes.explanation: Economy is the strength here. The word 'dibs' perfectly encapsulates the absurdity of local government dysfunction. Short, punchy, well-delivered as an unashamed statement of fact.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman
dialogue.line: You see, government appointments work through a careful vetting process, committee reviews, and extensive background checks.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman
dialogue.line: It's not like dibs. You can't just call it on a position.

jokes.text: 'Boring' is my middle name, so... my thoroughly vetted candidate is going to blow your candidate out of the water.
jokes.setup: A councilman dismisses Leslie's call for proper interviews as 'boring'
jokes.punchline: Leslie owns 'boring' as a badge of honor with full Leslie Knope bravado, immediately pivoting to a competitive threat
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie character moment — she turns an insult into a point of pride with characteristic enthusiasm. Not particularly original but well-executed character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Proper process is so boring.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Boring is my middle name.

jokes.text: Ron! You redacted all the information. / I answered some of them. / For 'date of birth,' you wrote 'springtime.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to check Ron's medical form
jokes.punchline: Ron has literally redacted his own medical paperwork like a classified government document, and his answer for date of birth is 'springtime'
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Ron joke. The idea of Ron redacting his own medical paperwork is a perfect distillation of his character's libertarian paranoia about government (even when he IS the government). 'Springtime' as a date of birth answer is both absurdly vague and somehow poetic for Ron. Extremely character-specific — this joke could not exist without Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Ron, it says here under 'Do you have any allergies?' you wrote 'I am only allergic to incompetence and lack of ambition.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That is correct.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: But I need to know if you're allergic to any foods or medications.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: As I said, incompetence and lack of ambition. Also, possibly shellfish.

jokes.text: How many drinks of alcohol do you consume a week? / One. / That's it, one drink? / One shelf.
jokes.setup: Doctor asks Ron about weekly alcohol consumption
jokes.punchline: Ron's answer of 'one' sounds reasonable until clarified: one shelf of alcohol
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is flawless: 'one' reads as modest self-control, then 'one shelf' detonates. The comedic beat between the two lines is perfect. Economy is exceptional — the whole joke is four words total across two characters. Completely Ron-specific. Extremely quotable. This rivals the caliber of the 8.0 anchor example.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: One.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: One shelf. I don't get cute with words.

jokes.text: Do you exercise? / Yes. / Lovemaking and woodworking.
jokes.setup: Doctor asks Ron if he exercises
jokes.punchline: Ron's forms of exercise are lovemaking and woodworking
jokes.explanation: Another strong Ron answer. The joke works because both activities are deeply Ron-specific (his relationship with Diane, his famous woodworking) and the framing of them as exercise is both logical and absurd. The beat structure (yes, then the list) is clean. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I exercise twice a day. In the morning, I practice my woodworking. In the afternoon, I go to the gun range.

jokes.text: Do you have any history of mental illness in your family? / I have an uncle who does yoga.
jokes.setup: Doctor asks about mental illness history
jokes.punchline: Ron considers yoga to be a form of mental illness
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed. The question implies a medical seriousness; Ron's answer reveals his worldview: yoga practitioners are the mentally ill family members. Great economy, high character specificity, and the logic is both absurd and internally consistent for Ron. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no family history of mental illness. My father was very healthy, very strong. He once worked through a bout of what doctors called 'depression,' but he called it 'Mondays.' My mother had no problems whatsoever. She was a very stable person. Very calm. I consider yoga a mental illness.

jokes.text: Allergies? / Cowardice and weak-willed men. / And hazelnuts.
jokes.setup: Doctor asks about allergies
jokes.punchline: Ron lists character flaws as allergies, then adds 'and hazelnuts' as a mundane afterthought
jokes.explanation: Excellent three-part joke. The setup lets Ron give a grandiose, character-defining answer ('cowardice and weak-willed men'), which would be a complete joke on its own, then the 'and hazelnuts' grounds it back in the mundane and lands an extra beat. The structure (big abstract + small specific) is perfect and the hazelnut detail makes it feel true. Among the Ron medical exam sequence's best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm allergic to: lying, weak men, and artificial sweeteners.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And also peanuts.

jokes.text: Sexual history. / Epic and private.
jokes.setup: Doctor asks about sexual history
jokes.punchline: Ron's entire answer: 'Epic and private.'
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect joke. 'Epic and private' is both a complete statement of Ron's character and a total comedic deflection. The word 'epic' is doing enormous work — it's boastful but delivered with total dignity. Maximum economy. Extremely quotable; this is the kind of line that becomes a character signature.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Two-word summary that says everything and nothing

jokes.text: He's a rude, brash jerk. You'll love him.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Ron she's getting his doctor
jokes.punchline: Her glowing recommendation of the doctor is that he's 'a rude, brash jerk' — perfect for Ron
jokes.explanation: Nice joke about the Leslie-Ron relationship. Her accurate prediction that Ron will love a difficult doctor — because Ron IS a difficult doctor — shows her genuine understanding of him while being funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Charity is a great way to help your personal brand.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, I don't need charity. I'm very wealthy. I have a net worth of several million dollars.

jokes.text: I don't like charity. I don't get it. Feels to me like I'm giving money away, and getting nothing in return.
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom are pitching the Sweetums Foundation to Dennis Feinstein
jokes.punchline: Dennis states the concept of charity with complete literalism, finding it baffling
jokes.explanation: Good villain/antagonist establishment. Dennis's literal interpretation of charity as 'giving money away and getting nothing' is both accurate and completely tone-deaf, establishing him as the episode's comic foil.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to smile and nod, and when Dennis least expects it, I'll strike with bureaucratic precision.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: [to camera] The key is to never let them see you sweat. Dennis thinks he's intimidating, but he's never faced someone who knows the entire Pawnee municipal code by heart.

jokes.text: If I give as much as I get, I'm giving $20 million. Ay yi yi. That's how much I'm worth, 20...million...dollars.
jokes.setup: Ben suggests Dennis could help his personal brand by giving as much as he gets
jokes.punchline: Dennis announces his net worth with a dramatic pause between each word, as if $20 million is an unfathomable sum
jokes.explanation: The joke is Dennis's pomposity about $20 million — a modest sum for a 'mogul' — delivered like it's incomprehensible wealth. Functional character comedy, but the self-aggrandizement is a well-worn comedic territory.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Bill Gates? No, no, no. Mark Cuban.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mark Cuban? Oh, well that changes everything. I love Mark Cuban.

jokes.text: Ah, he's disgusting, but I want to take his money and give it to needy people, so I'm just gonna keep on smiling. Yay!
jokes.setup: Ben is visibly uncomfortable with Dennis Feinstein
jokes.punchline: Ben's talking-head confessional: grimly pragmatic acceptance of tolerating a horrible person for charity
jokes.explanation: Good talking-head beat. The 'Yay!' delivered with dead-eyed determination is the comedic engine here — Ben's forced cheerfulness while hating everything is a reliable Ben note. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Like Bill Gates. Have you ever heard of Bill Gates? He lives in Seattle, guy with glasses. / Bill Gates? I know who Bill Gates is. Bill Gates is, like, a super nerd. Is this some sort of nerd thing? Are you calling me a nerd?
jokes.setup: Ben mentions Bill Gates as an example of a philanthropist mogul
jokes.punchline: Dennis interprets 'Bill Gates' as an insult and gets paranoid that Ben is calling him a nerd
jokes.explanation: Nice character moment. Dennis's insecurity is revealed through his touchiness about being associated with 'nerds.' 'He lives in Seattle, guy with glasses' as an explanation of Bill Gates is a funny bit of condescension. The escalation to paranoia ('Is this some sort of nerd thing?') is good.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Harris, I see you're really excited about this position!

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: Oh, I am! I've always wanted to work here. This company means everything to me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great enthusiasm. Wait... didn't you work here before?

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but that was different. I'm ready to start fresh!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Harris, you were fired from here last month.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: ...I prefer to think of it as a temporary separation.

jokes.text: Uh, he meant Mark Cuban. / Cuban? Now, that's the kind of guy I can hang out with-- Mark Cuban. / I'm interested now. Keep talking.
jokes.setup: Ben's Bill Gates reference has gone sideways; Tom tries to salvage it
jokes.punchline: Swapping 'Bill Gates' for 'Mark Cuban' immediately transforms Dennis's hostility to enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Good Tom-saves-the-day moment. Tom's instinct to translate 'nerd billionaire' into 'cool billionaire' is perfectly in character for him. Dennis's instant mood flip is a solid comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: Brett? Brett Knope?

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Harris! Oh man, it's been forever!

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: I know! What have you been up to?

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Just living life, you know? Be excellent to each other.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: Did you just quote Bill & Ted?

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Party on, dudes.

jokes.text: Stay still. 'Don't think about how much this itches.' That's very good advice.
jokes.setup: Doctor examines Ron and tells him not to think about the itchiness
jokes.punchline: Ron evaluates the advice with the same serious consideration he'd give a military order: 'That's very good advice.'
jokes.explanation: Good Ron beat. His clinical evaluation of obvious, self-evident advice ('that's very good advice') is funny because of the formality with which he delivers it.

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: I went to a four-year college.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's great! What school?

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: Prison.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's only four years if you're convicted of a felony.

jokes.text: I have to say, this is the greatest search committee ever assembled to find a new Animal Control Department head. Chris Traeger can do more with one foot than most people can do with three.
jokes.setup: The search committee is assembled; it consists of Chris (on crutches with a broken foot) and April
jokes.punchline: Chris's absurdly enthusiastic self-assessment: he can do more with ONE foot than most people can do with THREE (an impossible standard)
jokes.explanation: Classic Chris Traeger hyperbole. The logic 'more with one foot than most people can with three' is absurd because no one has three feet — he's comparing himself to an impossibility. Perfectly in character for Chris's relentless positivity taken to illogical extremes.

jokes.text: I'm not going to lie to you. I needed that. / I know.
jokes.setup: Chris compliments April as 'beautiful' and 'talented'
jokes.punchline: Chris admits he needed the encouragement he was giving April; April responds with knowing weariness: 'I know'
jokes.explanation: Good Chris/April dynamic. His neediness and her flat acknowledgment of it is a well-established comedic pairing. 'I know' from April is perfectly deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: I've been seeing a therapist.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's awesome! I love that. Therapy is amazing. It's like you're part of an exclusive club where everyone's working on themselves. We're all just trying to be the best versions of ourselves together. It's beautiful, really.

jokes.text: April Ludgate is beautiful... / Stop. / You are talented... / No.
jokes.setup: Chris tries to compliment April for the committee
jokes.punchline: April cuts off each compliment with flat rejection ('Stop.' 'No.') — then accepts the one about animals
jokes.explanation: Good April character moment. Her rejection of standard compliments but acceptance of 'passionate about animals' is a perfect character reveal — she hates empty praise but responds to genuine specificity. The rhythm of compliment/stop/compliment/no is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: Wait, what kind of animals are we talking about here?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Just the usual park animals. Squirrels, birds, the occasional deer.

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: Do you have any surgical tools on site?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Uh, no. Why would we have surgical tools?

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: And your security system—does it have blind spots near the perimeter?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I think we're done here.

jokes.text: But most importantly, you're passionate about animals. / That's true. It's because I'm half wolf.
jokes.setup: Chris says April is passionate about animals
jokes.punchline: April explains it's because she's half wolf
jokes.explanation: Perfect April joke. Delivered with total conviction as if it explains everything. 'Half wolf' as a sincere self-identification is deeply on-brand for April's gothic weirdness. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: I'm a certified psychic. I can read minds, predict the future, commune with spirits.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Orin, you're not a psychic.

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: I knew you were going to say that.

jokes.text: Wassup? I'm Harris. I'm 33 years young. I have my cousin Jason's truck for two more weeks. I have one testicle-- whac-a-mole accident-- and I'm down to clown.
jokes.setup: Donna says she'll send in the best candidate from the resumes
jokes.punchline: The best candidate is Harris, who was just fired, delivering a job interview intro that escalates to 'one testicle -- whac-a-mole accident'
jokes.explanation: Outstanding escalation joke. The intro starts as a bizarrely casual job interview and builds to 'one testicle -- whac-a-mole accident' which is not only absurd but includes 'whac-a-mole accident' as a parenthetical clarification as if that's the important context. The callback structure (he was literally just fired by these people) adds another layer. 'Down to clown' as a professional closer is perfect. One of the episode's highest-impact moments.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Open wide and say 'ahh'.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is poplar? You're using poplar? A government doctor using poplar wood. I could've made a better tongue depressor from a pine branch I found in the parking lot. This is an embarrassment.

jokes.text: Harris, we know who you are. I literally just fired you. / Oh, is this that job? That's crazy! Never mind.
jokes.setup: Harris introduces himself as if he doesn't recognize the committee
jokes.punchline: He doesn't realize this is the same job he was just fired from, and when told, responds with 'That's crazy! Never mind.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Harris's complete unawareness that this is the same job, and his casual 'Never mind' exit as if his application was a detached business proposition, is great character consistency. The confusion reads as genuine rather than played, which is funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Well, he left before I could tell him the results. Probably for the best. I don't really like patients anyway.

jokes.text: What up? Yo, my name is Brett. I like burgers, and also, I'm very high right now.
jokes.setup: After Harris is dismissed as the 'best' candidate, the committee wonders who's second
jokes.punchline: Brett walks in with an equally terrible self-introduction, including volunteering that he's currently high
jokes.explanation: Good parallel joke to Harris's intro. 'I'm very high right now' as a job interview disclosure is great. The structure mirrors Harris's intro (name, random personal detail, confession) in a way that feels like these two have the same broken template for self-presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I read that vaccines cause autism.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Well, that's been thoroughly debunked by science.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I read it on the internet.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: That doesn't make it true.

jokes.text: Dude, this is hilarious! / Oh, yo! We live together! / Yo, we live in the same place! / This is my boy! / Hey, 'Wyld Stallyns'!
jokes.setup: Harris and Brett are both called in as the top two candidates
jokes.punchline: They have a joyful reunion as if they haven't seen each other in years — they live together
jokes.explanation: Fun visual moment. The 'Wyld Stallyns' reference (Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure) as their self-styled duo name adds a layer of absurdist self-mythology. Their complete obliviousness to the context (job interview) is well-maintained.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Our new initiative has been incredibly successful. We've seen a 47% increase in community engagement and participation rates are through the roof.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait... those numbers are actually the pothole complaints. We've made things worse.

jokes.text: You guys know why there are all those cops out there? / Where are the cops at? / I gotta go. / Yo.
jokes.setup: Harris and Brett are in the middle of their reunion
jokes.punchline: Harris casually mentions seeing cops outside, Brett's instant response is panic ('Where are the cops at? I gotta go'), and they immediately exit
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic exit. Brett's instant fight-or-flight panic at the mention of cops, combined with Harris's complete calmness about mentioning it ('you guys know why'), is a perfect two-character comedic moment. The abruptness of their exit is the joke. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I hunt foxes. It's a very old tradition. You ride horses, you wear red coats, you have dogs chase the fox until it's exhausted, then you kill it. It's elegant, really.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Of course, sometimes the fox fights back. Scratches you up real good. And if you're not careful, it can bite your... well, let's just say I've had to see a doctor about fox bites in places I'd rather not discuss with a lady.

jokes.text: Guys, we're going out. Let's scent up! / I call dibs on 'Ooze.' / I got 'Money Shot.' / Yeah. / I got 'Blood Spurt.' / Ooh, no, don't use that one. / Eh, go ahead.
jokes.setup: Dennis invites the group to dinner and tells everyone to 'scent up'
jokes.punchline: The cologne names escalate from gross to disturbing: 'Ooze,' 'Money Shot,' 'Blood Spurt' — with conflicting advice about Blood Spurt
jokes.explanation: Good escalating cologne-name joke. 'Money Shot' and 'Blood Spurt' are progressively wrong for a luxury product. 'Ooh, no, don't use that one / Eh, go ahead' is a nice comedic button with the conflicting advice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm not fast. I'm just really good at hiding.

jokes.text: Well, I love cats, and dogs sure are great.
jokes.setup: A candidate is being asked why they want to work in Animal Control
jokes.punchline: Their entire qualification and motivation is stated in the most generic, minimal terms possible
jokes.explanation: Functional comedy from the parade of terrible candidates. The utter lack of enthusiasm ('dogs sure are great') is mildly funny but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dennis, you've been a total jerk to everyone today.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Me? I'm just living my life according to my principles.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What principles? You told Jerry his hair looks like a dead animal.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Exactly. Honesty is a principle. I'm actually the moral one here.

jokes.text: Well, you have all the qualifications. You went to a four-year college. / Actually, when I went there, it was just a two-year college. / Wow, so you're not even technically qualified to work at your current job.
jokes.setup: Chris enthusiastically notes the candidate went to a four-year college
jokes.punchline: The candidate reveals the college was two-year when he attended — meaning he doesn't even meet the qualifications for the job he currently has
jokes.explanation: Nicely constructed. The reversal (qualification becomes disqualification, and retroactively for his existing job) is a good comedic structure. Chris's immediate pivot to salary reduction ('we're going to have to lower your salary / Oh, well, fair's fair') is a great secondary beat.

dialogue.speaker: Vern
dialogue.line: I work at a place called 'Silly Willy's Wiggly Worm Wonderland.' It's a children's activity center.

jokes.text: You're fired. Get out. / No, no, you're not fired, but we're definitely going to have to lower your salary. / Oh, well, fair's fair.
jokes.setup: The candidate has been revealed to be under-qualified even for his current job
jokes.punchline: The candidate accepts his salary reduction with total equanimity: 'Oh, well, fair's fair'
jokes.explanation: Functional secondary beat. The candidate's resigned acceptance is mildly funny but not exceptional. April's quick 'You're fired. Get out.' is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I guess you could say this interrogation is really... *Vern*-ing out of control.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: *smiles proudly at own joke*

jokes.text: I am very, very, very, very frightened of animals.
jokes.setup: A candidate is being interviewed for Animal Control
jokes.punchline: He reveals he is 'very, very, very, very frightened of animals'
jokes.explanation: Good escalating beat in the awful-candidates montage. The quadruple 'very' conveys genuine terror and is funnier than a single 'very' would be.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not a pun, that's a double entendre. And a weak one at that. A pun is a play on words with multiple meanings. What you did was just say something mildly suggestive. It's like the difference between a well-crafted knife and a butter spreader. Both cut, but only one has any real utility.

jokes.text: You see Dr. Richard Nygard? I'm a Nygardian too!
jokes.setup: A terrified candidate mentions his therapist, Dr. Richard Nygard
jokes.punchline: Chris shares the same therapist and immediately bonds over it, using 'Nygardian' as a cult-like identity
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chris character joke. His enthusiasm for shared therapy is perfectly in character, and coining 'Nygardian' as a group identity (like a religion or fan club) takes a relatable premise to an absurd extreme. Very Chris-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I got you these luxurious hand creams and moisturizers.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would you do that? I like my hands rough and calloused. They're a sign of hard work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But they're so dry and cracked.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the point. Soft hands are for people who don't do anything.

jokes.text: Would you sign my cast? / Yes, but just please don't give me this job.
jokes.setup: Chris and the candidate have bonded over their shared therapist
jokes.punchline: The candidate asks Chris to sign his cast (treating him like a celebrity) and begs not to be hired
jokes.explanation: Nice absurdist beat. The interview has completely derailed into a therapy-support-group dynamic. 'Please don't give me this job' as the candidate's sincere request is a good subversion — usually candidates want jobs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I anticipated you'd reject all the conventional beauty products, so I made some alternatives.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is a mud mask made from actual mud. From a swamp. That I found.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And this is a moisturizer made from rendered animal fat and tree bark.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Finally, something I can get behind.

jokes.text: The spaying and neutering tools, do you think those fit humans? / Mm-mmm. Mm-mmm. Mm-mmm. / And is there a lock on the spaying room door? / Mm-mmm. Mm-mmm.
jokes.setup: A candidate inquires about the tools and facilities
jokes.punchline: The questions reveal disturbing interest in using animal spaying/neutering equipment on humans — April's repeated 'mm-mmm' is increasingly alarmed
jokes.explanation: Effectively dark and disturbing. The escalating implication (the questions progress from 'do they fit humans' to 'is there a lock') builds genuine discomfort. April's increasingly horrified 'mm-mmm' responses are funnier than any dialogue would be.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not going to answer that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, um, why not?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Because you already know my name. We work together. If you didn't know my name by now, that would be sad. For you.

jokes.text: Hello, Orin. Thank you so much for applying, now leave. / Hey, give him a chance. / What makes you qualified for animal control? / I studied zoology in college, and I can control animals with my mind. / Get out. / I made you say that.
jokes.setup: April's creepy acquaintance Orin applies for the job
jokes.punchline: Orin claims to control animals with his mind, then claims he made April say 'get out' with his mind
jokes.explanation: Great Orin joke. His claim of psychic animal control is absurd, but 'I made you say that' is the gem — it retroactively reframes April's dismissal as confirmation of his powers. Unfalsifiable and perfectly delivered. 'I liked him' from April (presumably) adds a great button. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I need you to do the hearing. I'm like a baby Bjorn and you're the baby, and if you don't testify, I'm going to have a very uncomfortable rash.

jokes.text: I liked him.
jokes.setup: Orin has just been ejected from the interview after claiming to control minds
jokes.punchline: April, who told him to leave, immediately says she liked him
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word button on the Orin scene. April being the one who wanted him gone but then endorsing him is completely in character — she appreciates the genuinely weird and unsettling. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine, I'll do the hearing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really? Oh my god, thank you so much!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: But I have one serious condition.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Anything, name it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You have to promise me that you'll never, ever get married.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why would you—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Because if you marry Ben, I will literally kill myself.

jokes.text: Balsa wood? You could at least use mahogany.
jokes.setup: The doctor breaks something (a tongue depressor or similar tool) while examining Ron
jokes.punchline: Ron's complaint is not about the examination but about the quality of wood used in medical instruments
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron woodworking character joke dropped into an unexpected context. His professional offense at balsa wood being used when mahogany is available is a perfect character tic. Very quotable and extremely Ron-specific.

jokes.text: There's something occluding your ear. / It's sawdust. Just blow.
jokes.setup: Doctor finds something in Ron's ear during examination
jokes.punchline: It's sawdust — confirming Ron's woodworking hobby has literally infiltrated his body
jokes.explanation: Good Ron character detail. The sawdust in his ear is a natural extension of his woodworking identity — he is so absorbed in his hobby that it has physically entered him. 'Just blow' as the casual instruction is a nice matter-of-fact touch.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Drinking under the age of 21 is actually really cool and—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: —illegal and wrong and something that I, as a government official, cannot condone in any...

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: —way. Thank you.

jokes.text: Wish all patients were like that. It's really annoying when they ask questions.
jokes.setup: Ron has demanded his test results and walked out
jokes.punchline: The doctor wishes all patients were as incurious and dismissive as Ron
jokes.explanation: Good character pairing joke. The doctor is revealed to be as anti-patient-engagement as Ron is anti-medical-care — they're perfectly matched cranks. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: It's like she's a ventriloquist and April is the dummy, except the dummy is better at talking.

jokes.text: You know, they claim that smoking is bad for you, but is there any medical evidence to back that up? / Great point.
jokes.setup: Dennis makes a casual comment about smoking
jokes.punchline: He questions whether there's medical evidence that smoking is bad — and gets validation from one of his sycophants
jokes.explanation: The 'rich idiot denies science' joke is fairly well-worn territory. Dennis's sycophant validating the claim adds a layer but doesn't elevate it significantly. Functional, gets a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'd like to make a donation to the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yes, here's a check for one million dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Just kidding. It's fake. You're all idiots. I'm never donating anything.

jokes.text: I have my own foxes flown in from Russia. We drug them pretty heavily so they can't get very far. In fact, mostly, they just flop around on the ground. Makes it easier to just walk up and 'pow!' Stupid foxes. It's deeply erotic.
jokes.setup: Dennis mentions fox hunting and explains his process
jokes.punchline: His 'fox hunting' is heavily drugged foxes that can barely move, culminating in 'Stupid foxes. It's deeply erotic.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest Dennis moments. The escalation is perfect: Russian foxes → heavily drugged → flopping on the ground → 'just walk up and pow!' → 'Stupid foxes.' Each element adds to the portrait of Dennis's twisted recreation. 'It's deeply erotic' as the final tag is the perfect capper — completely unexpected, making it somehow more disturbing than it already was. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Your cholesterol is very low.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is cholesterol?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: It's a waxy substance found in your blood.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you're talking about.

jokes.text: That sounds amazing. We should go hunting sometime. I'd love to. / I could bust out my Ralph Lauren Fall 2010 collection. Copped it in 2012. Clearance rack!
jokes.setup: Dennis invites Tom to go hunting with drugged foxes
jokes.punchline: Tom's idea of hunting attire is clearance rack Ralph Lauren from 2012 (purchasing the Fall 2010 collection two years late)
jokes.explanation: Good Tom character detail. His fashion aspirations (Ralph Lauren) undercut by his budget reality (clearance rack, two seasons late) is a perfect Tom Haverford note. The specificity ('Fall 2010 collection. Copped it in 2012.') makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not you, April. It's me. I'm withdrawing my application.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Is there someone else?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Because I saw you talking to that girl from the other department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We had something special, Leslie. You were going to change the world, and I was going to watch you do it and occasionally say something mean.

jokes.text: Wear whatever you want, as long as it's not too bright or reflective. You know, I want you blending in to the surroundings. / How fast can you run? / I think that guy wants to hunt me.
jokes.setup: Dennis gives suspiciously specific instructions about Tom's hunting outfit
jokes.punchline: Andy quietly observes that Dennis wants to hunt Tom — a paranoid reading that turns out to be completely reasonable
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy setup. Dennis's instructions (no bright colors, blend in, how fast can you run?) are so obviously threatening that Andy's 'I think that guy wants to hunt me' is simultaneously paranoid and completely accurate. 'How fast can you run?' is the perfect escalating detail. Great economy in Andy's observation — delivered as quiet terror.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I'm voting for April's idea. And before you ask why, it's because I'm an opportunist and I saw which way the wind was blowing. Also, I just made up a term called 'retro-jammed' and I'm going to use it at least five more times today.

jokes.text: So, Dennis, not to interrupt-- / Then don't. Boom! Ha ha! / Shut him right down!
jokes.setup: Ben tries to redirect the conversation back to the charity pitch
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts him off before he can even start and celebrates doing so: 'Boom! Ha ha!'
jokes.explanation: Good Dennis character moment. His self-congratulatory 'Boom! Ha ha!' at a minor victory is perfect for his personality. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's not a Rolex Mobile, it's a Lexus.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: If a Rolex costs $10,000 and a Lexus costs $30,000, how many Rolexes would you have to steal to equal the price of one Lexus?

jokes.text: I have heard so much talking from you. I don't want to hear your fat mouth say anything else.
jokes.setup: Dennis is increasingly hostile to Ben
jokes.punchline: His dismissal escalates to the gratuitously personal 'your fat mouth'
jokes.explanation: Functional antagonist line but 'fat mouth' as an insult is fairly generic. The joke is Dennis's villainy rather than anything particularly clever. Below average for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So what are these new powers exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you can make anyone do whatever you want.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Leslie, make Ben apologize to me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, apologize to April.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, April.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Now make him give me a thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, give April a thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Now make him kiss me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, kiss April.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not doing that.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, I thought you said I could make anyone do whatever I want?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I can't actually do that. I'm just a middle manager at Parks and Rec.

jokes.text: You're a dick. / Excuse me? / Andy-- / How dare you talk to me like that? Where are your manners? You come to me asking for money, and you treat me like this?
jokes.setup: Dennis has been insulting the group; Andy has been quietly watching
jokes.punchline: Andy, who was told to say nothing, delivers the honest verdict everyone was thinking: 'You're a dick.' Dennis's outrage is the secondary joke.
jokes.explanation: Great Andy moment. He was explicitly told to watch and learn, and his contribution is this perfect, unvarnished assessment. The dramatic irony (we all agree with him; the consequences are dire) makes it land hard. Andy's obliviousness to decorum is his defining trait, perfectly deployed here.

jokes.text: Mr. Palletta, what is your occupation currently? / I run a children's break dancing studio called 'D.J. Jazzy Vern's.'
jokes.setup: Leslie interviews Councilman Jamm's candidate for Animal Control director
jokes.punchline: His current occupation is running a children's break dancing studio named after himself
jokes.explanation: 'D.J. Jazzy Vern's' is a funny specific detail — the DJ Jazzy Jeff reference slightly off-center, and the possessive apostrophe suggesting pride of ownership in a children's dance studio. Good comedic naming.

jokes.text: Do you have any experience with animals? / Uh, a bat landed on my face once.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Vern about his experience with animals
jokes.punchline: His entire animal experience is a single incident where a bat landed on his face
jokes.explanation: Good minimal joke. 'A bat landed on my face once' is specific, weird, and clearly involuntary — it's the opposite of animal control experience. Good economy.

jokes.text: Hey, you know what, he's not a rack of ribs, so stop grilling him. / Nailed it. / Ribs are better smoked than grilled, so un-nailed it, with the back part of the hammer.
jokes.setup: Jamm defends his candidate with a barbecue metaphor
jokes.punchline: Vern prematurely celebrates the pun; Leslie corrects the culinary inaccuracy of the metaphor and 'un-nails it' with a hammer analogy
jokes.explanation: Excellent three-beat joke. The setup is a straightforward barbecue pun. The middle beat (Vern saying 'Nailed it') is a premature victory lap. The punchline is Leslie factually correcting the culinary inaccuracy of the metaphor and constructing a new meta-metaphor ('un-nailed it, with the back part of the hammer'). The structure is inventive — a joke that gets corrected into a better joke. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jamm said if I got my teeth whitened, I'd just get the gig.
jokes.setup: Vern is in the middle of an interview for Animal Control director
jokes.punchline: He reveals Jamm promised him the job in exchange for teeth whitening — Jamm gave him the gig for being a dental patient
jokes.explanation: Good callback confirming the worst about Jamm's appointment process. The corruption is petty and dental-related, perfectly consistent with Jamm's character. Solid callback structure.

jokes.text: Not bad, right? I mean, if he can catch raccoons as well as he can teach six-year-olds to pop and lock, he's a home run. / That is an insane statement.
jokes.setup: Jamm advocates for Vern's candidacy
jokes.punchline: His rationale — children's breakdancing skills transferring to animal control — is accurately described by Leslie as 'an insane statement'
jokes.explanation: Jamm's logic is hilariously non-sequitur. 'That is an insane statement' is a perfectly calibrated straight-man response — it acknowledges the joke without overselling it.

jokes.text: I don't like lotion. I like my hands to be cracked and calloused like a railway worker. / I know. I filled the bottles with fake blood, vinegar, and mud.
jokes.setup: Leslie gives April a gift of lotion bottles
jokes.punchline: Leslie has customized the lotion with April-specific contents: fake blood, vinegar, and mud
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a beautiful piece of character comedy about the Leslie-April relationship. Leslie knows April so well that she customized a gift to be anti-comfortable. 'Fake blood, vinegar, and mud' is specific enough to feel researched. April's 'Really? Thanks.' is the perfect response — genuine gratitude from April, which is rare. The joke illuminates their friendship beautifully while being funny. High character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: I nominated you for the position, and your confirmation hearing is in three minutes. Surprise. / No, I don't want the job. You can have your mud and blood back.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been buttering April up with the customized gift
jokes.punchline: The gift was a setup — the hearing is in three minutes — and April immediately offers to return the 'mud and blood' gift in protest
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure. April's 'You can have your mud and blood back' as a rejection of the gift/manipulation is a solid comedic beat that also demonstrates she understands exactly what happened.

jokes.text: Let's practice. What's your name? / Batman. See? I failed.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to practice the confirmation hearing with April
jokes.punchline: April answers 'Batman' and immediately declares herself failed
jokes.explanation: Good April joke. The self-assessment ('See? I failed') after choosing an obviously wrong answer demonstrates her combination of awareness and intentional non-compliance. Short and punchy.

jokes.text: I will be your Pocahontas. Climb into my papoose. Please do this. Please, please. Do it. Do it. Do it. You're gonna do it.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to convince April to do the confirmation hearing
jokes.punchline: Leslie's motivational speech devolves into 'Climb into my papoose' — a culturally confused metaphor — followed by increasingly desperate pleading
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie character moment. 'Climb into my papoose' is a wonderfully specific and confused metaphor for Leslie's supportive enthusiasm. Her desperate repetition ('Do it. Do it. Do it.') is endearingly manic. Very Leslie-specific.

jokes.text: Okay. / Yes! Yay! / But only if you divorce Ben. / Hey, don't even joke about that. / What? I really think he's wrong for you.
jokes.setup: April agrees to do the hearing; Leslie celebrates
jokes.punchline: April's condition is that Leslie divorce Ben; when Leslie protests, April insists she's serious
jokes.explanation: Good April joke. Her insistence on the divorce condition as legitimate ('I really think he's wrong for you') blurs the line between joke and genuine April weirdness. Characteristic of her dry, deadpan relationship with Leslie.

jokes.text: Okay. Let's tear this chick a new one, shall we?
jokes.setup: The confirmation hearing resumes
jokes.punchline: Jamm's opening statement as a committee member is to enthusiastically announce his intention to destroy the candidate
jokes.explanation: Functional Jamm villain beat. His enthusiasm for cruelty is on-brand but not particularly inventive here.

jokes.text: Ms. Ludgate, we have found many emails showing how you sexually harassed Leslie Knope's assistant. / Andy? That's my husband. / They were still extremely graphic, and appreciated by all of us. I had never heard of several of those terms, and I'm a freak.
jokes.setup: Jamm presents evidence of April 'harassing' an assistant
jokes.punchline: The assistant is her husband Andy; Jamm's response is that the emails were 'graphic' and 'appreciated by all' including himself — 'and I'm a freak'
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating joke. The setup (harassment allegations) inverts when it's revealed to be her husband. Jamm's response ('appreciated by all... and I'm a freak') takes it to a new and unexpected place — his self-identification as 'a freak' as a credential for evaluating content is hilarious. The 'I had never heard of several of those terms' adds depth. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Easily. Alcohol is delicious and fun... / [pause — Leslie speaks instead of April] / ...damentally a substance that should not be abused.
jokes.setup: Jamm challenges April about drinking alcohol as a minor in City Hall
jokes.punchline: April begins to enthusiastically defend alcohol ('Easily. Alcohol is delicious and fun...') then Leslie cuts in to finish the sentence as '...damentally a substance that should not be abused'
jokes.explanation: Outstanding structural joke. The setup lets April start a genuinely incriminating answer, then Leslie hijacks it mid-word to pivot it into a complete 180 — making 'fun...' become 'fun-damentally a substance that should not be abused.' The construction is near-perfect: the word split is clever (fun/fundamentally), the two characters' voices merge seamlessly, and the follow-up 'Ms. Ludgate, are you a ventriloquist?' makes the gag explicit in a great callback beat. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Wow. Ms. Ludgate, are you a ventriloquist? I mean, that is amazing how you make your words come out of Ms. Knope's mouth. Would you like to put her on your knee?
jokes.setup: Leslie has just finished April's sentence for her
jokes.punchline: A councilman plays along with the 'ventriloquist' framing, suggesting Leslie is the dummy ('Would you like to put her on your knee?')
jokes.explanation: Good follow-through on the ventriloquist premise. The joke reverses who is the dummy (putting Leslie on April's knee rather than the other way around) in a way that's both structurally sound and character-appropriate — April IS the more dominant personality in this dynamic.

jokes.text: Leslie, no one needs to be jammed today. / Okay, all we need is some kind of distraction. Grab that gavel and break your other foot.
jokes.setup: Leslie is panicking that April is failing the hearing
jokes.punchline: Leslie's solution is for Chris to deliberately break his other foot with the gavel as a distraction
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy. 'Break your other foot' as a tactical suggestion is both callous and brilliantly specific — it would work as a distraction, which makes the logic funny rather than just mean. 'I like the idea of double the signings' response is a great Chris beat.

jokes.text: I like the idea of double the signings, but I think the negatives outweigh the positives.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests Chris break his other foot for a distraction
jokes.punchline: Chris actually considers it as a proposal — 'I like the idea of double the signings' — but logically rejects it
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chris character joke. His genuine cost-benefit analysis of breaking his own foot — finding a silver lining (double cast signings!) before rejecting it — is perfectly in character for his relentlessly positive, logical nature. Great economy.

jokes.text: I guess my first move as director would be to fill your office, house, and car with snakes, and then train a crow to fly up your butt.
jokes.setup: The council asks April to explain what she'd do as director
jokes.punchline: April's policy plan: snakes in Jamm's office/house/car + a trained crow to fly up his butt
jokes.explanation: Brilliant April answer. The escalation from 'fill your office with snakes' to 'and your house' to 'and your car' is good, but the pivot to training a crow for a specific anatomical destination is the gold. The specificity ('fly up your butt') rather than any more graphic phrasing is funnier for its clinical matter-of-factness. Very quotable, deeply April-specific.

jokes.text: This check is made out to 'Go [bleep] yourself.' / In your face! Dennis Feinstein helps no man! Get the hell out of my office!
jokes.setup: Dennis apparently forgave Andy's outburst and gave the group a check for $25,000
jokes.punchline: The check is made out to 'Go [bleep] yourself' — it was a fake-out — followed by Dennis's declaration 'Dennis Feinstein helps no man!'
jokes.explanation: Great misdirection. The scene has played as a redemption arc — Andy apologized, Dennis forgave, check was presented — so the reveal ('Go [bleep] yourself') is a perfect subversion. 'Dennis Feinstein helps no man!' as his credo is wonderfully grandiose and quotable. The bleep adds rather than detracts by forcing the imagination. Strong misdirection structure.

jokes.text: Why did you make me apologize to him? / Guys, just hold it-- hold on a sec. / Mr. Feinstein, with all due respect... you are a major dick. / What? / Run! / Eddie, get my crossbow. / Crossbow? What the-- / You will pay for this!
jokes.setup: The fake check reveal causes chaos
jokes.punchline: Ben calls Dennis a 'major dick,' prompting Dennis to send for a crossbow and declaring 'You will pay for this!' — escalating to potentially lethal consequences for charity solicitation
jokes.explanation: Good escalating scene. The crossbow is a wonderful specific escalation — not a gun, a crossbow, suggesting medieval preparation. 'Crossbow? What the--' as a reaction captures the audience's surprise. Ben finally calling Dennis a 'major dick' after being told not to say anything is a satisfying character moment.

jokes.text: Hey, you look better. / I guess actual medicine can be effective. Who'da thunk? / Please leave me alone.
jokes.setup: Ron has been to the doctor and clearly feels better
jokes.punchline: Ron's acknowledgment that medicine worked is delivered with the maximum possible reluctance: 'I guess actual medicine can be effective. Who'da thunk?'
jokes.explanation: Good Ron character beat. His grudging admission that medicine works, framed as a shocking discovery ('Who'da thunk?'), is perfectly in character. The immediate 'Please leave me alone' as a follow-up is a great Ron button.

jokes.text: Your cholesterol is 120, which is the lowest I've ever seen. / What's 'cholesterol'?
jokes.setup: Doctor gives Ron's test results
jokes.punchline: Ron has never heard of cholesterol — implying his lifestyle is so analog/pure that he has no concept of it
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron joke. The punchline works on multiple levels: his perfect cholesterol (a paradox given his diet of red meat) and his complete ignorance of the term. Ron's body being inexplicably healthy despite his lifestyle is a running character absurdity, and 'What's cholesterol?' is the perfect non-sequitur response to good news.

jokes.text: And the only problem I see is that your potassium's low, so just eat a banana once in awhile. / No, thank you. I live the way I live, I eat the things I eat, and I'll die the way I'll die.
jokes.setup: Doctor's only medical advice is to eat a banana
jokes.punchline: Ron declines a banana with a full philosophical statement about living and dying on his own terms
jokes.explanation: Strong Ron joke. The existential gravitas applied to refusing a banana is perfectly in character — Ron treats minor life decisions with the same weight as major philosophical positions. 'I'll die the way I'll die' as the conclusion to a banana refusal is absurdly proportionate. Quotable.

jokes.text: That's oddly beautiful... but also stupid.
jokes.setup: Ron makes his dramatic statement about living and dying on his own terms
jokes.punchline: The doctor's reaction: 'That's oddly beautiful... but also stupid'
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic response. The pause before 'but also stupid' deflates the grandeur of Ron's statement beautifully. Good economy — acknowledges the character's appeal while puncturing his pomposity.

jokes.text: You're not alone in the world anymore, Ron. You're dating a woman who has two kids, so every three days, think about Ivy and Zoe and Diane, and eat a damn banana.
jokes.setup: Ron refuses the doctor's banana advice
jokes.punchline: Leslie's emotional appeal escalates to 'eat a damn banana' — the banana as the object of the most sincere speech in the scene
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Leslie's genuine emotional appeal about Ron's girlfriend and children is delivered sincerely, making the 'eat a damn banana' punchline funnier by contrast. The fruit has accumulated comedic weight through the scene, so the button lands well.

jokes.text: That is a genius idea. Somebody wake up Milton. History is being made. / Iwo Jima!
jokes.setup: April proposes absorbing Animal Control into Parks
jokes.punchline: Milton, who has been asleep, wakes up shouting 'Iwo Jima!' — apparently mid-dream
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the earlier Milton-is-asleep detail. 'Iwo Jima!' as his waking exclamation is perfectly specific — his dreams are WWII battles. The timing (being woken for 'history being made' and producing this) is well-structured.

jokes.text: Look at that, April. You won over Jamm. / Uh, no, she didn't. I'm just sick of being on the losing side. I'm going to tell everyone this was my idea. Retro-jammed.
jokes.setup: Leslie observes that April's idea has won Jamm's support
jokes.punchline: Jamm clarifies he hasn't changed — he's just repositioning, and has coined 'Retro-jammed' for retroactively claiming others' ideas
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jamm character joke. 'Retro-jammed' is a genuinely inventive coinage — Jamm has created a verb for retroactively claiming credit, using his own name. The joke reveals character (his shamelessness), creates a new piece of vocabulary, and is perfectly concise. Very quotable. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Uh, no, she didn't. I'm just sick of being on the losing side. I'm going to tell everyone this was my idea. Retro-jammed.
jokes.setup: Leslie says April won over Jamm; Jamm corrects her
jokes.punchline: 'Retro-jammed' — Jamm's neologism for claiming retroactive credit for others' ideas — is a self-coining that reveals his entire character philosophy
jokes.explanation: Justifies 8+: 'Retro-jammed' is an excellent neologism — Jamm has coined a term for his specific brand of credit-stealing, using his own name as the verb root. The fact that he announces the concept as if coining it in real time ('I'm going to tell everyone this was my idea. Retro-jammed.') shows absolute shamelessness. The word rewards replay and is highly quotable. Character integration is near-perfect — only a politician named Jamm would turn opportunism into a branded maneuver.

jokes.text: What do we do now? Can I apologize again? I'm getting really [good] at apologizing.
jokes.setup: The group has just escaped Dennis Feinstein's crossbow
jokes.punchline: Andy's solution/skill development update: he's getting good at apologizing and offers another one
jokes.explanation: Good Andy callback. His framing of forced apologies as a skill he's developed is characteristically oblivious and endearing. The enthusiasm for his new ability is very Andy.

jokes.text: Screw that. You should apologize for apologizing to that guy.
jokes.setup: Andy offers to apologize again
jokes.punchline: Ben's position: the apology itself was the wrong move — meta-apology required
jokes.explanation: Functional beat. The meta-apology logic is mildly funny but not particularly inventive. Good economy.

jokes.text: Feinstein's the worst. I hope he gets into an accident driving that Rolex Mobile. / For the last time, it's a Rolexus, and you can't drive it.
jokes.setup: The group vents about Dennis Feinstein
jokes.punchline: Tom corrects Ben's misremembering of 'Rolexus' as 'Rolex Mobile' with pedantic insistence, and adds the technical detail that 'you can't drive it'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Tom defending the correct terminology for a ridiculous object, and clarifying that the Rolexus is non-functional as a vehicle ('you can't drive it'), doubles down on the absurdity from earlier. 'For the last time' implies this has already been corrected multiple times off-screen, which is an extra layer.

jokes.text: Rent-A-Swag is gonna donate five cents from every dollar we make this month. It's not Feinstein money, but it'll help.
jokes.setup: The team has lost the Feinstein donation
jokes.punchline: Tom's generous gesture: five cents per dollar (a 5% donation) from a small clothing rental business
jokes.explanation: Warm Tom character beat. The modesty of the donation (5%) from a modest business is funny for its proportionality. Not a strong joke but a good character moment.

jokes.text: At Leslie's suggestion, I have made you deputy director of Animal Control within the Parks Department. You'll be amazing at it, and the best part, there is no confirmation hearing. / How did you make this plaque so quickly? / I had it made your first week here. I knew you'd be going places, so I wanted to be prepared.
jokes.setup: Ron presents April with a plaque naming her deputy director
jokes.punchline: He had the plaque made in her first week — Leslie knew from the beginning where April would end up
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny character moment. Leslie's preemptive plaque preparation is a perfect expression of her character — obsessive preparation combined with genuine faith in her people. The comedic element is the slightly terrifying level of advance planning.

jokes.text: How did you make this plaque so quickly? / I had it made your first week here. I knew you'd be going places, so I wanted to be prepared.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents April with a deputy director plaque
jokes.punchline: The plaque was made during April's first week — Leslie's obsessive preparation and belief in those she mentors is revealed as having existed for years before the moment
jokes.explanation: The pre-made plaque is very Leslie — her confidence in people she believes in extends to material preparation years in advance. It's both funny and warm, which is the Parks and Rec signature. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Can I hire an intern? / Not yet. / Can I hire a Mexican elf? / No. / Can I buy a child bride? / No. / Then how is this even a promotion?
jokes.setup: April is told she can't hire an intern in her new role
jokes.punchline: Her escalating list of requests ends at 'child bride' — and when all are denied, she questions the value of the promotion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. The escalation from reasonable (intern) to absurd (Mexican elf) to deeply inappropriate (child bride) is perfectly calibrated, and Ron's consistent flat 'No' to each is the straight-man anchor. 'Then how is this even a promotion?' as a genuine grievance is the perfect button — it's completely logical from April's perspective. Very April-specific. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Government shouldn't operate based on personal favors. It should operate based on good ideas. April had the best idea, and today the best idea won. / Leslie, I really have to go to the bathroom. / Oh, yeah, right, sorry.
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a triumphant speech about government and good ideas
jokes.punchline: Ron deflates the moment by announcing he needs the bathroom; Leslie immediately defers
jokes.explanation: Good scene-closing deflation. Ron undercutting Leslie's triumphant moment with a bathroom need, and Leslie immediately treating it as the priority, is a great character dynamic beat.

jokes.text: You don't have to come in with me. / I wasn't going to. / Could you pick up the pace a little bit? / Oh, yes, Miss Daisy.
jokes.setup: Leslie is helping Ron (who was sick) to the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Ron tells Leslie she doesn't need to accompany him; when she asks him to hurry, he responds with 'Oh, yes, Miss Daisy' — sarcastically adopting the role of a chauffeur to her Lady
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, yes, Miss Daisy' is a good Ron retort — sardonic, literary, slightly unexpected. The Driving Miss Daisy reference (Ron as reluctant servant/she as imperious passenger) is an apt and funny inversion of their actual relationship.

tmdb_overview: Leslie decides to give the Animal Control Department a much-needed makeover. Ann tries to get Ron the medical attention he needs. Ben, Tom, and Andy recruit donors for their charity foundation.
insight: Animal Control escalates character absurdism through 59 jokes—Parks' densest episode yet at 2.21 per minute.
